newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open unchanged before CPI, sales.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open unchanged before CPI, sales.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices opened unchanged on Tuesday ahead of government reports on U.S. price and retail sales trends in December.
The December U.S. Consumer Price Index (CPI) will be released at 0830 EST/1330 GMT, as will the December retail sales report.
"The market is going to be little changed until we see the numbers," said Kim Rupert, senior economist at MMS International.
Economists in a Reuters poll have forecasted, on average, that the CPI rose 0.3 percent in December after a 0.3 percent November rise.
Without the more volatile food and energy components of the index, the CPI should be up 0.2 percent for December, just as it was in November, they said.
Economists estimated, on average, that retail sales rose 0.5 percent in December after a 0.4 percent November decline.
Without autos, retail sales are expected to be up a moderate 0.4 percent in December after a smaller, 0.3 percent November rise.
A smaller than expected retail sales increase could generate a bounce in the Treasury market, participants said.
"We think we'll get a slightly below consensus retail sales gain of about 0.1 percent with a 0.5 percent gain ex-autos," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at I.D.E.A.
Stiles said a bounce on a sluggish retail sales report would run into resistance "up around 110-24 to 111 on the March T-bond contract."
Rupert said MMS was looking for a slight 0.2 percent rise in retail sales and a 0.3 percent increase without auto sales.
"If we get those numbers, we rally a bit," she said. She also defined resistance levels at 110-23 on the March T-bond contract and then 111 even.
With regard to the CPI, however, the market will be less patient than it once might have been of a higher than consensus reading, said Stiles.
"There will be less tolerance for an above consensus CPI since we have a good economy in place and because of the hourly earnings trend, which was up 3.8 percent in 1996," he said.
Higher inflation in conjuction with a brisk pace of economic growth could cause more participants to worry that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates.
Federal Reserve Chairman's speech in Belgium generated no market reaction, analysts said.

"He was talking about general central banking themes for G-10," said Stiles. "He said there was progress against inflation but warned against complacency and said central bankers should err on the side of caution. There was nothing seen in those comments to move the market."
"He was quite general and offered nothing specific on the U.S. economy," said Rupert.
The market also gets data on December real earnings and the Atlanta Fed Index at 1000 EST/1500 GMT.
Two weekly reports on department and chain store sales are also due.
The BTM/Schroders index of chain store sales is rumored to be down 0.3 percent, on the soft side.
In early trade, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was up 1/32 to 95-18/32, yielding 6.85 percent.
Two-year notes were up 1/32 to 99-15/32, yielding 6.04 percent. Three- and six-month bill rates were unchanged at 5.06 percent and 5.11 percent, respectively.
Five-year notes were up 1/32 to 98-29/32, yielding 6.38 percent.
Ten-year notes were up 1/32 to 99-6/32, yielding 6.61 percent.
